It carries more weight at this step than any other single answer, and that isn't our opinion: pilots who've flown both these classes argue endlessly about which actually feels calmer in bad air, and what that disagreement settles is that your own sense of control in rough air tells you more than the letter on the wing does. Build it in small doses: light bumps at a familiar site, hands working, with a coach or experienced pilot nearby and a clear plan for getting down if it builds. A sports psychologist who coaches pilots recommends exactly that — repeated small steps outward rather than one big one — and treats the hesitation itself as useful information rather than something to override. Until it feels different, the more forgiving wing is the right one to be building it on.

source.cites: "The community thread on 'High End Bs vs. Low EN Cs' shows pilots disagreeing about which actually feels calmer in bad air... This argues for the app weighting the pilot's own reported comfort/control in rough air fairly heavily at this step, rather than leaning only on the EN letter." Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz Episode 109 (expert, sports psychologist) treats fear as a protective signal to work with rather than override and recommends deliberate mini-steps outward. XC Mag's 'The Head Game' (industry/expert, Thomas Theurillat) frames readiness as challenge matched to honest self-assessed skill, with too big a jump producing stress rather than growth.
source.note: Framed around behaviour under load rather than around feeling afraid, and explicitly does not reassure a hesitant pilot toward upgrading — required by docs/design-context.md, whose terminology appears nowhere in the body.

suggestions.title: Start debriefing the ones you don't understand
suggestions.body: A few near misses you can't explain is the clearest thing on this list to act on. Write up what happened as soon as you land — conditions, what you did, what surprised you — then go through them with an instructor or an experienced pilot. Unexplained incidents tend to repeat, and the ones you can explain usually stop. Two of the instructors behind the advice in this tool work exactly this way with pilots, and one of them built his own recovery after a serious collapse on it. It matters more at this step than at the ones below, because the class you're looking at gives you less time to work out what's happening in the moment — you want the pattern recognition already built.

source.cites: Bendicht Erb via Podz-Glidz Episode 35 (expert, instructor and certified sports psychologist) works on structured processing of incidents and describes rebuilding after his own low-altitude double frontal collapse; Yvonne Dathe via Podz-Glidz Episode 109 (expert) works the same way with pilots in her coaching practice. The final clause rests on the EN-C certification language about precise pilot input being required for recovery.
source.note: At mid-B to high-B this suggestion leans on Flybubble's 'incident-free thermic hours' qualifier, which belongs to that step's figure rather than this one. Here the justification is the reduced margin instead, which is this step's own material.

suggestions.title: If this matched what you already suspected, that's worth something
suggestions.body: Pilots are often right about their own readiness before a tool tells them. If "not yet" or "nearly" is roughly what you expected, treat that as good judgement rather than a setback — a sports psychologist who works with pilots is explicit that deciding not to fly, or not to upgrade yet, when your honest self-assessment doesn't match the wing or the day is sound judgement, not something to be embarrassed about. There's no hurry built into this step either. Every source on progression pace assumes one rung at a time, this particular rung is the one the industry argues about most, and the pilots who fly these wings keep repeating the same thing: being under-prepared for a C costs you more than spending another season on a B. Almost everything that genuinely makes you better — centring climbs, reading the day, launches, knowing when not to fly — is the same work on every wing, so none of that time is spent waiting.

source.cites: The safety guard: a 'not yet' result must land as a legitimate, successful outcome of using the tool, never as a failure or something to be argued out of.
source.note: The specific supports are knowledge/steps/high-b-to-low-c.md#psychological--mindset-factors (Yvonne Dathe, expert sports psychologist, on choosing not to fly or not to upgrade as sound judgement), the same file's collapse-handling section (the asymmetric-risk consensus), knowledge/disagreements.md point 3 (this is the most contested boundary) and point 13 (every source addressing progression pace assumes one rung at a time). No internal terminology used. Shares the 'under_load' topic with 'nerves_are_not_the_problem', which outranks it for a pilot who has that specific gap.
